The route is important for air travellers, who had raised concerns over the safety of the road and asked GMR authorities to take up repairs immediately.
Vizianagaram Collector S. Ramsundar Reddy had reportedly alerted the executives of the group to the damage, pointing out that many VIPs travel the route.
He asked them to verify the reasons for the damage of the road, which happened within three months after the inauguration of the airport.
With pressure from government, the contractors took up repair works temporarily and assured to relay the road shortly.

article_sentences: Andhra Pradesh has submitted a preliminary Cyclone Arnab damage report to the Centre.
The Rs 4,600 crore estimate underscores extensive infrastructure and agricultural losses.

Andhra Pradesh has submitted a preliminary report to the Centre estimating that very severe cyclonic storm Arnab caused damage worth Rs 4,600 crore in the state, Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu said on Friday, according to news agency Press Trust of India.
Naidu assured compensation and relief for affected families, farmers and fishermen.
He said seven people were killed in the cyclone despite precautionary measures and announced compensation of Rs 5 lakh for each bereaved family.

Speaking to reporters after visiting a cyclone shelter at Matrevu in West Godavari district, Naidu said the government was working to restore essential services and assist people who had suffered losses.
"The preliminary assessment puts the damage caused by very severe cyclonic storm Arnab at Rs 4,600 crore.
We have submitted the report to the Centre and will ensure compensation and relief reach all affected families, farmers and fishermen," Naidu said, according to PTI.
He said the government had coordinated preparations across departments before the cyclone.
Officials were kept on alert through repeated teleconferences and overnight reviews.
The administration also monitored the possibility of heavy inflows into reservoirs and tanks to prepare for potential flooding.
Power infrastructure suffered extensive damage, with more than 15,000 electricity poles uprooted across the affected areas.

stories.headline: Flood Control in Jhelum: HC seeks report on mining activities, STPs, embankments
stories.title: Flood Control in Jhelum: HC seeks report on mining activities, STPs, embankments
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 30: The High Court of Jammu and Kashmir has sought a report attesting to mining activities, proposed setting up of Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs) in river Jehlum as also construction or removal of embankments for flood control of the waterbody. A division bench comprising Chief Justice Dr Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Yash Paul Bourney sought the report after Advocate Nadeem Qadiri assisting as amicus curiae in the Public Interest Litigation (PIL) by Environmental Policy Group on conservation of Jehlum, raised these issues. “What is the kind of legal or illegal mining activity is going on in the entire river Jhelum? How many STPs have been proposed to be established in the course of river Jhelum? And how many of the embankments have been built or removed for the purpose of containing the flood?” the amicus said at the very outset. Following the Court counsel’s submission, senior Additional Advocate General for the government informed the court that he would respond to all the issues. Furthermore, he would explain the execution of the affidavit filed by the Divisional Commissioner on October 25, he said The Court however directed the senior AAG to indicate also the milestones achieved so far in the matter related to flood mitigation. It listed the matter for further hearing on October 31. Filed in 2017, the PIL flags the fragile flood management system in Kashmir. It seeks the court's intervention for measures to protect Kashmir from future flood disasters. The PIL also highlights the shortcomings in flood management due to which massive damage was caused during 2014 floods and seeks tangible steps to avoid such situations.

stories.headline: Israel: Heading to another election?
stories.title: Israel: Heading to another election?
stories.summary: The elections to the 120-member Israeli Knesset which were held on October 27 were closely watched in the region. This was primarily because they were expected to indicate the support which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had among the Israeli people for the pursuit of the Iran war. Netanyahu’s Likud party along with its rightwing coalition partners went all out to woo voters to their cause but the result was fractured. It demonstrated the political and social contentions within Israel in general and also on the Iran war. Israeli elections are held on a proportional basis. That means that voters do not vote for particular candidates but for political parties. Generally, each party, even in a coalition, puts up separate lists. The number of seats allotted to a party depends on the number of votes it has got provided it crosses the threshold of 3.25 % of the total vote. The entire country is treated as one constituency. The result of this complex election process is that no single party succeeds in getting a majority on its own strength. Hence, coalitions are formed. The coalition situation prior to the October 27 election was thus: Netanyahu’s Likud led party coalition had 68 seats. It had won 64 seats in the 2022 elections but four members of another party had later joined it to raise its number to 68; the Jewish opposition parties 42 and the two Israeli-Arab parties 10. The results led to a sharp drop in the Netanyahu led Likud party coalitions. It secured only a vote share which would give it 53 seats. Meanwhile the Jewish bloc which is now under the leadership of former head of the Israeli defence forces, Gadi Eisenkot managed to get 48 seats based on its vote share. At the same time there was a dramatic increase in the share of the Israeli Arab parties from 10 to 19. The consequence of this break-up is that no coalition has sufficient number of seats to form a government on its own. It also means that Netanyahu has suffered a definite reverse but it has not been strong enough to oust him. This reverse has led the Israeli Prime Minister to claim that Qatar has sought to manipulate the election. On their part the Qataris have angrily and outrightly denied this charge. Most Israeli officials have rejected the charge of foreign manipulation in the election. However, Justice Noam Scholberg who was head of the Central Election Committee overseeing these elections claimed, according to news reports, that he had been shown some “exceptionally grave” information of foreign funding coming to these elections by Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security agency. Consequently, he has asked for Shin Bet to give its findings within the next few days. Clearly, the target of this charge of foreign funding are the Israeli Arab parties. On their part they have denied them. However, one Likud party spokesman was quoted in the media as saying “The Ra’amgate scandal is a political earthquake. Israel’s elections have been stolen!” Ra’am is one of the Arab parties. Meanwhile, while going along with the Shin Bet investigation Israel’s President Isaac Herzog has said that an entire community should not be tarnished for exercising its right to vote. The fact is that Israeli Arabs came out in record numbers to vote. That can be attributed to their anger with Netanyahu over the manner in which he conducted the campaign in Gaza after the horrific terrorist attack by Hamas on October 7, 2023. It is not only the Israeli Arabs but other sections of Jewish opinion which while outraged by Hamas terrorism were deeply disturbed by the disproportion of the Netanyahu led government’s response. They too may have swelled up the Israeli Arab parties’ numbers. Some analysts are viewing the Likud charge of foreign funding and interference in the election as a Netanyahu tactic to ensure that the Eisenkot led coalition does not even think of joining hands with the Israeli Arabs to seek to oust Netanyahu from power. In any event the prospect of the Jewish parties joining hands in a government with the Arab parties is remote. This is despite the fact that Israeli Arabs form around 20% of the country’s population. This is also because even though Israel projects itself as a democratic state which treats all its citizens equally it is in essence a Jewish state which is committed to protect the Jews especially in a land which the Jews believe was given to them by God. Israel’s Jewishness was consolidated by a ‘Basic Law’ enacted in 2018. That law proclaimed: “The land of Israel is the historical homeland of the Jewish people, in which the State of Israel was established. It also proclaimed that “The state’s language is Hebrew”. The only concession it made to Arab Israelis was “The Arabic language has a special status in the state; Regulating the use of Arabic in state institutions or by them will be set in law”. With 19 seats the Arab parties are now in a position to disrupt Israel’s political process. That is intolerable for most Jews. A number of options are under consideration of how the results of this election can be preserved. Under Israeli laws the President will be obliged to go through the motions of asking some leaders to form a coalition government. One can only be formed if some parties in Eisenkot’s coalition go to Netanyahu. That seems difficult to foresee but not as difficult as Eisenkot attracting the ultra-right-wing parties from Netanyahu’s coalition. Most likely Israel will head to another election. Meanwhile, Netanyahu will continue as a care-taker Prime Minister.

stories.headline: Bajaj, TVS, Hero post strong Q2 profit; industry sales grow 27 percent
stories.title: Bajaj, TVS, Hero post strong Q2 profit; industry sales grow 27 percent
stories.summary: The top three listed two-wheeler makers reported strong revenue growth in the September quarter as domestic demand, an export surge and fast-rising e-scooter sales outweighed a sharp rise in commodity costs. Margins and profit growth varied across the players.Bajaj Auto, the first among the three to report its results, posted its first-ever Rs 20,000 crore revenue quarter.Revenue from operations rose 34 percent to Rs 20,003 crore, and net profit rose 35 percent to Rs 3,354 crore. Ebitda climbed 37 percent to Rs 4,172 crore. The margin was 20.9 percent, up 40 basis points from a year earlier and flat from the June quarter. Total volumes rose 20 percent to 15.49 lakh units, led by exports.TVS Motor reported revenue of Rs 17,103 crore, up 44 percent, with Ebitda up 47 percent at Rs 2,219 crore. Its margin widened 30 basis points to 13.0 percent. Net profit rose 52 percent to Rs 1,377 crore. Sales reached a record 19.19 lakh units, up 27 percent.The country’s largest two-wheeler maker Hero MotoCorp had the weakest earnings growth of the three.Standalone revenue rose 21 percent to Rs 14,687 crore and Ebitda rose 8 percent to Rs 1,968 crore. Net profit grew 5 percent to Rs 1,456 crore. Its Ebitda margin was 13.4 percent, up 10 basis points from the June quarter but down about 164 bps YoY.On a consolidated basis, Hero’s profit rose 41 percent to Rs 1,861 crore, helped by a one-time Rs 397 crore gain from the equity dilution of an associate company after its capital raise.Even in terms of sales volumes, Hero had the weakest rise, with wholesale volumes up 10.5 percent to 18.68 lakh units.Explaining the reasons behind Hero’s Q2 performance, Jay Kale, Director-Institutional Equity Research at Elara Capital, said: "Hero’s EV business is just ramping up, so commodity pressures in terms of EV losses are higher for them compared to the others. For Bajaj and TVS, a better exports mix and favourable currency movement helped offset the rise in commodity costs.”Also Read: Bajaj Auto Q2 profit jumps 35 percent to Rs 3,353 crore as exports surgeIndustry DemandHero said industry retail sales rose more than 27 percent in the quarter, with internal combustion engine (ICE) models up 23 percent and electric vehicles up 82 percent.For the first half, retail rose over 20 percent, said Hero MotoCorp CEO Harshavardhan Chitale on a post-earnings call with analysts.“To understand the impact of pent-up demand of GST, we looked at growth over the two-year period [so as to strip out the impact], which was 11 percent CAGR. This shows that industry as a whole has a healthy growth momentum, even after discounting the impact of the pent-up demand,” he said.Bajaj said the industry, including electric scooters, grew 18 percent in April-August. On a post-earnings call, the management singled out motorcycles of 150cc and above and electric scooters as the main drivers.The GST cut that took effect on September 22, 2025, lowered the tax on smaller two-wheelers, and will make YoY comparisons harder in the second half.OutlookManagement at all three expect growth to slow from the pace witnessed in H1.Hero’s Chitale said he expects the industry to grow at mid-to-high single digits in the festive period and the second half. ICE models should grow at low single digits, with EVs lifting the overall number.TVS Managing Director K N Radhakrishnan, on an analyst call, said he expects “good single-digit” growth in the third quarter, citing a high base from last year.Bajaj Joint Managing Director Rakesh Sharma expects September-December growth to stay in double digits but below the April-August rate.Also Read: Ather Energy posts first profit as EV demand outstrips supplyRural DemandThe monsoon this year is the weakest in over a decade, with a 13 percent deficit in rainfall. Parts of India are also facing droughts.Hero said rural performance matched or beat urban in the quarter and so far in the festive period. Fears of a weak monsoon have not fully played out, with sowing close to last year’s level, it said.TVS said EV growth in rural markets was slightly higher than in urban markets in the first half.Bajaj was more cautious. Sharma said that drought-like conditions in Maharashtra, parts of the south and the northeast could hurt more in the fourth quarter. He said growth is skewed toward higher-income buyers, with entry-level products lagging, a “K-shaped” pattern that may get sharper.Input CostsBajaj said commodity and other input inflation was about 3-3.5 percent of revenue in the quarter, on top of about 4.5 percent in the first.The magnitude of this cost escalation is ‘unprecedented’, creating significant pressure on the business with inflation of a scale that we would typically see spread over many years, the management said.Price increases covered 50-60 percent of the impact in the first half. The balance was largely offset through favourable currency realisation and continued cost optimisation initiatives, it said.TVS said material costs rose about 1.9 percent from the June quarter, against price hikes of 1.6 percent. It has taken small increases in October and will review pricing after Diwali.Hero said commodity inflation was about 1 percent sequentially, and about half of the roughly 5.5 percent cumulative inflation in the first half has been passed on.It said margins should be stable in the third quarter and that Hero remains on track toward its 14-16 percent medium-term target.ExportsBajaj’s exports rose 41 percent to 7.79 lakh units, with shipments to Africa nearly doubling. Management said it aims to sustain about 7.5 lakh units a quarter. TVS reported record international sales of 5.39 lakh units, up 35 percent.Hero was the outlier. Its overseas dispatches fell about 24 percent to 85,000 units, hurt by port and customs disruption after an earthquake in a key Latin American market and weaker demand in Bangladesh after a fuel-price spike linked to the Gulf conflict. Colombia accounts for close to a quarter of Hero’s exports. Retail sales abroad still rose 19 percent, and Hero expects double-digit dispatch growth to return in the third and fourth quarters.Electric VehiclesEVs were the fastest-growing segment at all three companies. Bajaj’s electric two- and three-wheelers reached a record 2 lakh units, now a third of domestic revenue.Its Chetak scooter had its biggest quarter, with revenue above Rs 2,000 crore and a market share of about 23 percent. Bajaj said the EV business is now accretive to domestic margins but still dilutive for the company as a whole. Chetak capacity will rise to 80,000 a month by the fourth quarter.TVS sold 1.86 lakh electric two-wheelers, up 133 percent. Hero’s Vida retailed about 66,000 units, up 74 percent. Vida turned gross-margin positive, with its EBITDA drag narrowing to Rs 168 crore from Rs 232 crore in the June quarter.Hero’s EV market share was 11.1 percent in the quarter and about 13.5-14 percent in October so far. Hero plans to lift Vida capacity to 45,000 a month by the fourth quarter. Production-linked incentives helped all three, and Bajaj said it has reached the top PLI rate of 18 percent for the second half.PremiumisationBajaj is repositioning around motorcycles of 125cc and above. It chose to raise prices on 100cc models ahead of rivals and accepted weaker volumes there. Domestic two-wheeler volumes rose just 2 percent to 6.07 lakh units. It said refreshed Pulsars made up 33 percent of its 125cc-plus sales in the festive period so far. KTM and Triumph sold about 40,000 units, up 31 percent.Hero launched the Xtreme 160R and 250R in October and plans three to four more premium launches this financial year. It has 150 Premia stores. Premium market share was still just 1.9 percent in the first half. TVS is expanding Norton, though management conceded subsidiary losses are elevated. Scooters and EVs also lifted average realisations at all three companies.

stories.headline: From Indira to Modi
stories.title: From Indira to Modi
stories.summary: In a tight-spot after storm whipped up by the newly born Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) on the shear strength of Gen Z raking up NEET and other examination paper leaks, and related fallacies in the education system affecting the youth; although the issue was already being raised by Congress leader Mr Rahul Gandhi but got a fillip after the Gen Z movement. The Narendra Modi government and the ruling BJP-led alliance (though some of the ruling allies have exhibited their unease over the issue), has endeavoured to see red in the expression ‘regime change’. It seems to be an attempt to corner the opposition I.N.D.I.A bloc and the CJP, they have only talked about peaceful protest as means of change, through the narrative of ‘regime change’ and portray them as “working against the national interest”. The ruling dispensation of the current era (read BJP) have perfected the art of setting narratives and counter-narratives as diversionary tactics and as means to corner the political opponents. In the process, not minding even if the process becomes vicious. This process in itself seems to have reached a saturation stage and with entire gamut of SIR-related operation of the ECI getting public traction, they need to relook into this strategy with a positive frame of mind. Yes, Mr Gandhi, other leaders of the opposition alliance, CJP/other youth leaders and social activist/lawyer Mr Prashant Bhushan, have been facing a major political backlash from the BJP and indirectly from the government over remarks regarding “regime change”. The ire is directed more against them for targeting the Narendra Modi government under the garb of happenings in the ECI. Why has the word regime and phrase “regime change” suddenly become a hot potato for BJP to handle? Or does this reflect signs of insecurity for the “most powerful” government/ruling party in the world? What is the dictionary meaning of the word regime? It is just for the sake of clarity on something which is nothing new to be used in political parlance of the country and which found a greater expression in the then opposition leaders, including towering one of the then Bharatiya Jan Sangh (BJS) and now BJP, scathing attacks against Prime Minister Mrs Indira Gandhi particularly on imposition of internal emergency in 1975. The powerful opposition brigade using the term “Indira regime” (reference to the authoritarian nature of her administration) and the far-cry to oust it was led by Congress (O) leader and later Prime Minister Mr Morarji Desai. It included top BJS leader Mr Atal Bihari Vajpayee and Mr L K Advani, apart from Mr Jayaprakash Narayan who spearheaded campaign against Mrs Gandhi, another former Prime Minister Ch Charan Singh and socialist leader Mr Geroge Fernandes. And many others and including the maverick Mr Raj Narain who defeated Mrs Gandhi in Rai Barelli. According to AI a regime is a system or method of governing a country, organization, or institution, or the specific group of people currently holding power. The Cambridge dictionary terms it as a particular government or system or method of government. The Wikipedia defines it; in the context of national politics, it typically refers to the system of political organization that determines access to public office, and the extent of power held by officials. Does in any way, under the shadow of these definitions and given the history of Indira Gandhi-era, expression “regime change” reflect hatching of a conspiracy? It does not seem so. And on top of that a strong dispensation such as Narendra Modi government need not fear what at best could be the political usage of the expression. They have the wherewithal to expose conspiracy, if any. Political scientists often categorize regimes as being democratic, autocratic, or hybrid in the academic sense of the term. However, in everyday language, a regime is an authoritarian or unjust government. There is nothing unparliamentary or unconstitutional in these expressions which were very rightly used, at times even crossing limits of niceties, during the 1975-77 phase by the then opposition leaders and their young cadres. In the present context the ‘regime change’ mention has come in the light of alleged charges of manipulating electoral rolls with a motive to help the ruling party. Obviously, the reference has been made in order to build public opinion and convince the people that their votes could be safeguarded only through a ‘regime change’. The underlining factor is voter-lists without wholesale deletions and alleged arbitrary inclusions, and which are above any doubt. The BJP strategists seem to have lapped up the ‘regime change’ opportunity with both the hands. The party president, Mr Nitin Nabin led the charge through a post on ‘X’ which read; “The use of terms like ‘regime change’ has exposed the true agenda of the opposition….. This nefarious attempt to destabilise India in collusion with foreign powers is part of the agenda of ‘urban naxals’. The opposition’s fight is not for electoral reforms, SIR, or the future of the country’s youth… but rather to spread anarchy in the country and seize power at any cost.” Mr Nabin must decipher from the archives, as he was born in the year when the party which he heads now was born in 1980, as to how often phrase ‘regime change’ was used by his senior leaders and how often Mrs Gandhi and her coterie described the opposition’s movement as aided and abetted by foreign powers. Colourful theories were touted by the then opposition leaders as to how erstwhile USSR was helping Mrs Gandhi win elections through the use of a mysterious ink-pad and ballot paper; wherever you stamp it will appear on Congress symbol, was the oft repeated charge. Fact of the matter is that despite all such charges flying thick and high and the “mysterious foreign hand” at play, Mrs Gandhi lost the election in 1977, even losing her own seat. Majority of the opposition leaders including Mr Vajpayee and Mr Advani won the election to become Union Ministers for the first time. The ‘regime change’ had taken place through an impartial, free and fair election for which credit must go to Mrs Gandhi, notwithstanding excesses committed during the imposition of internal emergency. The ‘regime change’ did not connote any conspiracy at that point in time and the expression is finding place during the present movement against SIR and other failures of the government, in the same spirit. As a counter to BJP president’s assertion invoking “urban naxal and foreign powers” syndrome behind opposition’s ‘regime change’ metaphor, opposition is firm on its stand and so are the CJP activists. Mr Gandhi and other opposition alliance leaders maintain that their protests and criticisms are rooted in constitutional rights, democratic resistance, and fighting alleged capture of state institutions. And that there is nothing unconstitutional, illegal or anti-national in talking of a “regime change” using peaceful means through the expression of ballot.

The Wikipedia defines it; in the context of national politics, it typically refers to the system of political organization that determines access to public office, and the extent of power held by officials.
Does in any way, under the shadow of these definitions and given the history of Indira Gandhi-era, expression “regime change” reflect hatching of a conspiracy?
It does not seem so.
And on top of that a strong dispensation such as Narendra Modi government need not fear what at best could be the political usage of the expression.
They have the wherewithal to expose conspiracy, if any.
Political scientists often categorize regimes as being democratic, autocratic, or hybrid in the academic sense of the term.
However, in everyday language, a regime is an authoritarian or unjust government.

There is nothing unparliamentary or unconstitutional in these expressions which were very rightly used, at times even crossing limits of niceties, during the 1975-77 phase by the then opposition leaders and their young cadres.
In the present context the ‘regime change’ mention has come in the light of alleged charges of manipulating electoral rolls with a motive to help the ruling party.

This nefarious attempt to destabilise India in collusion with foreign powers is part of the agenda of ‘urban naxals’.

Majority of the opposition leaders including Mr Vajpayee and Mr Advani won the election to become Union Ministers for the first time.

The ‘regime change’ had taken place through an impartial, free and fair election for which credit must go to Mrs Gandhi, notwithstanding excesses committed during the imposition of internal emergency.

The ‘regime change’ did not connote any conspiracy at that point in time and the expression is finding place during the present movement against SIR and other failures of the government, in the same spirit.

As a counter to BJP president’s assertion invoking “urban naxal and foreign powers” syndrome behind opposition’s ‘regime change’ metaphor, opposition is firm on its stand and so are the CJP activists.

Mr Gandhi and other opposition alliance leaders maintain that their protests and criticisms are rooted in constitutional rights, democratic resistance, and fighting alleged capture of state institutions.

article_sentences: In what looks like a direct response to the ‘Russia Sanctions Act’ being signed into law that month, India in September 2026 slashed its oil imports from the U.S. to zero, and drastically cut down its imports of Russian oil, the latest official data shows.
Instead, India turned to the UAE for its oil requirement, with that country’s share rising to more than one-fourth of India’s oil imports.
As a result, India’s crude oil sourcing remains highly concentrated, with just two countries — Russia and the UAE — accounting for 60% of all oil imports.
The U.S. House of Representatives on September 16 passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which was then signed into law by President Donald Trump on September 18.
The law empowered the U.S. to levy tariffs of up to 100% on countries such as India and China that imported large quantities of Russian oil and gas.

The tariffs are currently in abeyance, with Mr. Trump on October 16 signing an executive order temporarily waiving the tariffs and submitting a certification to the U.S. Congress saying that the pause was in the U.S.’ national interest.
Indian government data on October oil imports will be released next month.
India imported 209.4 lakh tonnes of crude oil in September 2026, which was 9.5% higher than in August, and 4.1% higher than in September last year.

However, as has been the case in the last six months or so, elevated crude oil prices have meant that India’s oil import bill has swelled far faster than the growth in the actual quantity of oil being imported.

The data shows that India’s oil import bill of nearly $14.3 billion in September 2026 was 16.4% higher than the bill in August, and a much more significant 33% higher than in September 2025 when oil prices were relatively more benign.
Cooling off on Russian oil?
Russia’s share in India’s oil imports has recently been broadly following the U.S.’ actions regarding such imports.

stories.headline: The Mean Hides the Household
stories.title: The Mean Hides the Household
stories.summary: Ask anyone from the valley whether the economy is growing and the answer rarely matches the statistics. Both can be right. Economics separates what an economy produces from what a household can actually buy with what it earns, and the gap between the two is where the current argument sits. Let’s begin with the official account, because it is not a bleak one. The Jammu and Kashmir Economic Survey 2025-26 estimates real GSDP growth of 5.82 per cent and per capita income of Rs 1,68,243, and shows J&K’s per capita income rising from 71.9 per cent of the national figure in 2014-15 to about 76.5 per cent. That convergence is real and deserves credit. Yet the same document puts India’s real growth at 7.4 per cent, so the Union Territory is still growing more slowly than the country it is trying to catch. Purchasing power, though, is income measured against the price level. In plain terms, it is how much rice, fuel and rent a month’s earnings will cover. The Survey’s per capita figure is nominal, and it is an average. Two things can go wrong between that average and a household’s shopping basket: prices can outrun incomes, or incomes can fail to reach the household at all. The valley faces both risks. Take prices first. The Survey reports inflation easing from 4.5 per cent in 2024 to 3.8 per cent in 2025. That relief has not lasted. On the Ministry of Statistics’ new price index, J&K inflation was 1.34 per cent in January 2026 and 4.27 per cent in September, provisionally, with urban households at 4.65 per cent. Fairness requires saying that India as a whole is now at 5.54 per cent, so Kashmir is not the outlier this year. But a household feels a price level and the Survey concedes the level is high. Its consumer price index for agricultural labourers is the highest among a panel of nine states, with the food index second highest, both above the national average. Now the income side. A household lives on the earnings of its workers, so employment is the channel through which growth becomes purchasing power. The Ministry’s latest labour bulletin, for April to June 2026, shows an unemployment rate of 9.1 per cent in J&K for those aged 15 and above, against 5.4 per cent nationally. In urban J&K the rate was 14.9 per cent against 6.7 per cent, and for urban women 33.3 per cent against 8.7 per cent. Among those aged 15 to 29 it was 28.4 per cent against 15.9 per cent, rising to 41.5 per cent against 18.2 per cent in towns and cities. These are sample estimates, and the Ministry publishes their standard errors; the gaps are several times larger. The 6.1 per cent the Survey cites for 2023-24 rests on a one-year reference period, while the bulletin uses a one-week period, so the two should not be read as a trend. Nor is this a story of people staying home. Labour force participation among those 15 and above is 58.9 per cent in J&K against 54.6 per cent nationally. Kashmiris are looking for work. The work is not there in sufficient quantity. The Survey’s own numbers hint at why. Agriculture and allied activities employ 42.99 per cent of the workforce but generate 20.45 per cent of value added. Services produce 61.02 per cent of value added and employ 31.31 per cent. Economists call this a sectoral mismatch: people are concentrated where output per worker is lowest, and output is concentrated where jobs are fewest. Low labour productivity means low wages, and headline growth cannot lift household incomes when it accrues to sectors that hire few people. Then came a shock. Tourist arrivals fell from 2.36 crore in 2024 to 1.78 crore in 2025, a drop of roughly a quarter, and the Survey itself links a slowdown in services to subdued tourism activity after a recent untoward incident. Tourism accounts for nearly 7 per cent of GDP and about five lakh livelihoods. A demand shock to a sector that large does not stay in the sector. It travels through the multiplier to every local trader who sells to those households. The public purse cannot easily close the gap. Grants make up 56 to 66 per cent of resources and own revenue only 22 to 24 per cent. Salaries and pensions take 52.42 per cent of revenue expenditure. Capital expenditure, the spending that builds assets and creates jobs, had reached 42 per cent of last year’s total by November, against 64 per cent for revenue expenditure. Capital spending is usually heavier late in the year, so this may narrow, but it bears watching. What would help must work on both sides of the ratio. On prices, the Survey promises a logistics policy in 2026; it should be judged by whether it lowers the cost of moving goods into Jammu and Kashmir. On jobs, Mission YUVA’s target of 4.25 lakh jobs over five years offers a yardstick, and progress against it should be reported openly. On savings, banks held about ` 2.04 lakh crore in deposits in September 2025 but advanced ` 1.28 lakh crore, a credit-deposit ratio of 62.93 per cent. Local savings should finance local enterprise. And government should publish a regular, district-level real wage series, so that the question can be answered with data rather than argument. A per capita figure is an arithmetic mean, and a mean is true of nobody in particular. Jammu and Kashmir’s economy may well be growing; the Survey says it is. The test of whether that growth is working is whether a graduate in Srinagar can find a job, and whether a family’s rupee buys as much next year as it did this one. On the evidence the government itself publishes, the honest answer is: not yet. Malik Daniyal is a regular contributor to GK. He writes on the economics of valley.

sentences.text: On the Ministry of Statistics’ new price index, J&K inflation was 1.34 per cent in January 2026 and 4.27 per cent in September, provisionally, with urban households at 4.65 per cent.
On savings, banks held about ` 2.04 lakh crore in deposits in September 2025 but advanced ` 1.28 lakh crore, a credit-deposit ratio of 62.93 per cent.
Capital expenditure, the spending that builds assets and creates jobs, had reached 42 per cent of last year’s total by November, against 64 per cent for revenue expenditure.
The test of whether that growth is working is whether a graduate in Srinagar can find a job, and whether a family’s rupee buys as much next year as it did this one.
